title: Schemes · Isogeny Labs
description: A catalogue of cryptographic schemes, from RSA and elliptic curves to ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA and SQIsign: what each rests on, its standard, its sizes, the best known attack, and its status against quantum computers.
heading: Schemes
standfirst: What each widely used scheme rests on, what it costs, and where it stands against classical and quantum attacks. ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SQIsign have full pages; the rest are summarised here, with links to the attacks that set their parameters.

glance_blocks.p: "Broken by Shor's algorithm" means broken by a large fault-tolerant quantum computer, which does not exist yet. It is the reason for the move away from RSA and elliptic curves, and the reason key exchange moves first: traffic recorded today can be decrypted later, while a signature only has to resist forgery for as long as it is relied on.

groups.label: Key establishment
groups.intro: How two parties agree on a shared secret over a public channel: Diffie–Hellman key exchange, or a key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM), in which one side encrypts a fresh key to the other's public key.

entries.name: ECDH (X25519, P-256)
entries.summary: Diffie–Hellman on an elliptic curve. It is the standard key exchange in TLS 1.3, SSH and Signal, usually on Curve25519 as X25519.

facts.Rests on: The elliptic-curve Diffie–Hellman problem, which as far as anyone knows is as hard as the ECDLP
facts.Standards: RFC 7748 (X25519 and X448); NIST SP 800-56A with the curves of SP 800-186
facts.Sizes: X25519: 32-byte public keys and shared secret. P-256: 33-byte compressed or 65-byte uncompressed public keys
facts.Best known attack: Pollard's rho: about 2<sup>126</sup> to 2<sup>128</sup> group operations for 256-bit curves
facts.Quantum: Shor's algorithm; Roetteler et al. estimate about 2,330 logical qubits for P-256

entries.name: Finite-field Diffie–Hellman
entries.summary: Diffie and Hellman's original 1976 key exchange, in the multiplicative group of a prime field. Largely replaced by ECDH, which needs far smaller parameters for the same strength.

facts.Rests on: The Diffie–Hellman problem in F<sub>p</sub><sup>×</sup>, attacked through the discrete logarithm
facts.Standards: RFC 7919 named groups for TLS; NIST SP 800-56A
facts.Best known attack: The number field sieve, largely a precomputation on the prime that is then reused for every key; this is what the Logjam attack exploited. The record is a 795-bit prime field (2019)

entries.name: ML-KEM
entries.summary: The module-lattice KEM standardised in 2024, formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber. It is what replaces ECDH, at first alongside it as a hybrid.

facts.Rests on: Module learning with errors (MLWE)
facts.Best known attack: Lattice reduction
facts.Quantum: No known attack beyond small speedups to lattice sieving

entries.name: HQC
entries.summary: A code-based KEM that NIST selected in March 2025 as a backup to ML-KEM, chosen because it rests on different mathematics.

facts.Rests on: Decoding random quasi-cyclic codes
facts.Standards: Selected in NIST IR 8545 (March 2025). NIST expects to publish a draft standard and to finalise it in 2027
facts.Best known attack: Information-set decoding

entries.name: Classic McEliece
entries.summary: McEliece's 1978 code-based system, the oldest public-key design still considered secure: very large public keys and very small ciphertexts.

facts.Rests on: Decoding a random-looking binary Goppa code
facts.Standards: Under ISO standardisation. NIST's 2025 report (IR 8545) dropped it from NIST's current process, citing limited interest and the risk of an incompatible parallel standard, and said NIST may later base a standard on ISO's
facts.Best known attack: Information-set decoding, which decades of work have improved only modestly

entries.name: CSIDH
entries.summary: An isogeny-based key exchange with small keys and a property no lattice scheme offers: non-interactive key exchange, like Diffie–Hellman.

facts.Rests on: Inverting a commutative class-group action on supersingular curves over F<sub>p</sub>
facts.Best known attack: Classically about p<sup>1/4</sup>; quantumly, Kuperberg's subexponential algorithm, whose concrete cost is disputed
facts.Quantum: Subexponential; CSIDH-512 is widely considered too small

groups.label: Signatures
groups.intro: How a message is bound to a key, so that anyone with the public key can check it. Post-quantum signatures cost more bytes than the schemes they replace, by very different amounts:

chart.caption: Public key and signature sizes at the lowest standard security level of each scheme. SQIsign is at its round-3 parameters (version 3.0, September 2026); the ECDSA public key is compressed and its signature is the raw pair (r, s).

entries.name: RSA
entries.summary: The first widely deployed public-key system (1977), used for both signatures and encryption, and still common for signatures in web certificates.

facts.Rests on: The RSA problem, taking e-th roots modulo N = pq, which is no harder than factoring N
facts.Standards: PKCS #1 v2.2 (RFC 8017); FIPS 186-5 for signatures; SP 800-56B for key establishment
facts.Sizes: RSA-2048: 256-byte modulus and signature; RSA-3072: 384 bytes
facts.Best known attack: The number field sieve; the largest public factorisation is RSA-250, 829 bits, in 2020

entries.name: ECDSA
entries.summary: DSA on an elliptic curve, used in TLS certificates, hardware tokens, and the transactions of Bitcoin and Ethereum. Each signature uses a fresh secret nonce, and a nonce that leaks even a few bits loses the key.

facts.Rests on: The ECDLP, and a uniformly random secret nonce for every signature
facts.Sizes: P-256: 64-byte signature (r, s); 33-byte compressed public key
facts.Best known attack: Pollard's rho on the curve, about 2<sup>128</sup>. In practice, keys are lost to biased or leaked nonces through the hidden number problem

entries.name: EdDSA (Ed25519, Ed448)
entries.summary: Schnorr-style signatures on Edwards curves, with the nonce derived deterministically from the key and message, which removes the most common way ECDSA keys are lost.

facts.Rests on: The ECDLP on Curve25519 or Curve448
facts.Best known attack: Pollard's rho, about 2<sup>126</sup> for Ed25519. Deterministic signing is exposed to fault attacks instead

entries.name: Schnorr signatures (BIP-340)
entries.summary: Schnorr signatures on secp256k1, introduced to Bitcoin with the Taproot upgrade.

facts.Rests on: The ECDLP on secp256k1
facts.Best known attack: Pollard's rho, about 2<sup>127</sup> using the curve's extra automorphisms

entries.name: BLS signatures
entries.summary: Pairing-based signatures that aggregate: many signatures, even on different messages, combine into one short signature. Ethereum's consensus layer depends on this.

facts.Rests on: The computational Diffie–Hellman problem in the groups of a pairing, in practice on the curve BLS12-381
facts.Sizes: In Ethereum's choice, 48-byte public keys and 96-byte signatures
facts.Best known attack: Rho on the curve groups, and the number field sieve in the pairing's target field, which has embedding degree 12

entries.name: ML-DSA
entries.summary: The module-lattice signature standardised in 2024, formerly CRYSTALS-Dilithium: NIST's main replacement for RSA and ECDSA signatures.

facts.Rests on: Module learning with errors for the key; module short integer solutions for forgery
facts.Best known attack: Lattice reduction
facts.Quantum: No known attack beyond small speedups to lattice sieving

entries.name: FN-DSA (Falcon)
entries.summary: Hash-and-sign signatures over NTRU lattices: the smallest public key and signature of NIST's lattice schemes, with a harder signing algorithm.

facts.Rests on: Finding short solutions to linear equations over NTRU lattices (NTRU-SIS)
facts.Standards: FIPS 206, in preparation; NIST describes the process as under way
facts.Best known attack: Lattice reduction. Signing samples a discrete Gaussian with floating-point arithmetic, which makes safe constant-time implementations harder than for ML-DSA

entries.name: SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+)
entries.summary: Signatures built from a hash function and nothing else. It is the most conservative assumption available, paid for in signature size and signing time.

facts.Rests on: Security properties of the hash function, SHA-2 or SHAKE
facts.Sizes: SLH-DSA-128s: 32-byte public key, 7,856-byte signature. The 128f variant signs faster with 17,088-byte signatures
facts.Best known attack: Generic attacks on the hash function
facts.Quantum: Only generic speedups, which the parameters account for

entries.name: LMS and XMSS
entries.summary: Stateful hash-based signatures: small and fast, but each one-time key must never be used twice, so the signer has to keep reliable state.

facts.Rests on: Security properties of the hash function
facts.Standards: RFC 8554 (LMS) and RFC 8391 (XMSS); NIST SP 800-208, for uses such as firmware signing where state can be managed
facts.Sizes: Depend on the tree height and Winternitz parameter
facts.Best known attack: Generic attacks on the hash, or, in practice, a signer that reuses state

entries.name: SQIsign
entries.summary: Isogeny-based signatures with by far the smallest public key and signature of any post-quantum candidate, and slow, intricate signing.

facts.Rests on: Computing the endomorphism ring of a supersingular elliptic curve
facts.Standards: A round-3 candidate in NIST's additional-signatures process (NIST IR 8610, May 2026)
facts.Sizes: Version 3.0, level I: 83-byte public key, 200-byte signature
facts.Best known attack: Wesolowski's 2026 algorithm, in time and memory p<sup>1/3+o(1)</sup>; version 3.0 raised its parameters in response

groups.label: Symmetric ciphers and hashes
groups.intro: Schemes with no public key. They carry the bulk of the data once a key is agreed, and quantum computers threaten them far less: Grover's algorithm at most square-roots the cost of a key search, and parallelises badly.

entries.name: AES
entries.summary: The block cipher behind most bulk encryption, usually in GCM mode.
entries.quantum_short: Key search sped up by Grover, not broken

facts.Rests on: Twenty-five years of cryptanalysis; there is no reduction to a number-theoretic problem
facts.Best known attack: Biclique cryptanalysis recovers an AES-128 key in about 2<sup>126.1</sup> operations, four times faster than brute force. In practice, table-based software leaks through cache timing; use AES instructions or bitsliced code
facts.Quantum: NIST uses key search on AES-128 as the benchmark for its lowest post-quantum security category

entries.name: ChaCha20-Poly1305
entries.summary: A stream cipher and a one-time authenticator, designed to be fast and constant-time in software without special instructions.
entries.quantum_short: Key search sped up by Grover, not broken

facts.Rests on: Cryptanalysis of the ChaCha permutation, and the security of Poly1305 as a one-time authenticator
facts.Best known attack: Published attacks reach 7 of ChaCha's 20 rounds

entries.name: SHA-2
entries.summary: The SHA-256 and SHA-512 family, used almost everywhere a hash is needed.

facts.Rests on: Cryptanalysis of the compression function
facts.Best known attack: None on the full functions; collisions exist only for reduced-round versions. The Merkle–Damgård structure allows length extension, which is why keyed hashing uses HMAC

entries.name: SHA-3 and SHAKE
entries.summary: Keccak, a sponge construction chosen by public competition in 2012. Its extendable-output forms SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 run inside ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA.

facts.Rests on: Cryptanalysis of the Keccak-f permutation
facts.Sizes: 224- to 512-bit output, or any length for SHAKE
facts.Best known attack: Only reduced-round versions

groups.label: Broken or retired
groups.intro: Schemes that fell, and what finally ended them. Most of these failures were visible years before they became practical.

entries.name: SIKE
entries.summary: Supersingular isogeny key encapsulation, a fourth-round candidate in NIST's process, broken in 2022 in about an hour on a laptop.

facts.Rests on: An isogeny problem made easier by the torsion-point images the protocol publishes
facts.What ended it: The torsion-point attacks of Castryck and Decru, Maino and Martindale, and Robert, all in 2022
facts.Status: Withdrawn; the attack is polynomial-time, so larger parameters do not help

entries.name: Rainbow
entries.summary: A multivariate signature scheme and finalist in NIST's third round, broken in 2022.

facts.Rests on: Solving structured systems of multivariate quadratic equations
facts.What ended it: Beullens' 2022 key-recovery attack, which broke the level-I parameters in about a weekend on a laptop

entries.name: DSA
entries.summary: The original Digital Signature Algorithm (1991), over a prime field.

facts.Rests on: The discrete logarithm in a subgroup of F<sub>p</sub><sup>×</sup>, and a random nonce per signature
facts.What ended it: Not an attack: FIPS 186-5 (2023) no longer approves DSA for generating signatures, only for verifying old ones
facts.Status: Retired in favour of ECDSA, EdDSA and ML-DSA

entries.name: SHA-1
entries.summary: The 160-bit predecessor of SHA-2.

facts.What ended it: The first public collision in 2017 (SHAttered), then chosen-prefix collisions in 2020, which make forged certificates practical
facts.Status: NIST plans to retire it from all uses by 31 December 2030

entries.name: MD5
entries.summary: A 128-bit hash function from 1992.

facts.What ended it: Collisions found by Wang and collaborators in 2004, and chosen-prefix collisions from 2007; the Flame malware used one to forge a Microsoft code-signing certificate in 2012
facts.Status: Broken for any use that needs collision resistance

entries.name: DES and Triple DES
entries.summary: The 1977 block cipher standard and its tripled extension.

facts.What ended it: DES's 56-bit key was searched exhaustively in public in 1998. Triple DES's 64-bit block allows birthday attacks on long sessions, demonstrated as Sweet32 in 2016
facts.Status: NIST disallowed Triple DES for encryption after 2023

entries.name: RC4
entries.summary: A stream cipher once used in both TLS and WEP.

facts.What ended it: Biases in its keystream, which make plaintext recovery from many encryptions practical
